query.query: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers

title: Scalable, Fast Simulation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Scaled dot-product attention can be rewritten exactly as a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) whose weights are generated from the context at run time: the query is the input, the keys form the first layer, the values form the second, the exponential is the activation and the hidden width equals the context length. This fast-weight reading links the 2017 Transformer to fast-weight programmers from the early 1990s, to the key-value view of feed-forward layers, and to recent efficientattention designs, which either compress the growing MLP into a fixed-size module or route each query to a small part of it. We review this literature and find that its central claims are mostly stated in algebra or measured on large benchmarks where many factors change at once; it lacks a small, controlled test of what each design gives up. Starting from the XOR artificial neural network, we show that its hidden layer is a key-value lookup and that unnormalized linear attention, like a single perceptron, cannot compute XOR. We then implement eight token mixers inside an otherwise identical one-layer model and train them on in-context associative recall, where every sequence carries a fresh key-value table. All runs use three seeds on a CPU and are released as a tutorial notebook. The equivalence holds to machine precision, and the 1991 outer-product programmer matches unnormalized causal linear attention to 7 × 10-13. A model with slow weights only stays at chance (0.4%), so recall depends on fast weights. A ReLU activation works almost as well as softmax (99.5% at N = 256 facts), showing that the activation is not special but the growing width is. Compressed memories follow a crosstalk law (N-1)dv/d that we derive and verify, and both linear variants fall below 9% at N = 256 with d = 64. Per-query top-k routing is lossless, even when applied to a model trained with full attention (k = 1 keeps 99.99%), whereas routing to blocks or pooled landmarks reaches only 37-39% on unstructured contexts.</jats:p>

items.abstract: The subject here is system’s shaping of the subject of culture, literature, and liberalism—the modern self. Narrow-but-deep selves emerged from system’s role in mediating the formation of narrow-but-deep disciplines. With Mary Hays supplying a primary example, the chapter shows that when systems are extended through disciplinary travel so that they can no longer do what isolated systems do—they talk to themselves, the parts making a whole—another kind of self must be formally interpolated to do the talking. Embedded systems yield a newly expressive “I”—that is why in blaming The System we are also somehow blaming ourselves. This chapter bookends the tale of system and self by juxtaposing An Account of the Fair Intellectual-Club” from 1720 to Douglas Englebart’s report on Augmenting Human Intellect from 1962. In the former, young women try to improve themselves through system—both by forming a “club” as a social incarnation of system and by writing systems. In the latter, Englebart describes a “system” in which humans improve themselves by interfacing with technology. The presentation of this report announced the invention of the computer mouse. The chapter concludes by showing how issues of gender and privilege, secrecy and privacy, individual and national development, mix with new kinds of order and method generated by system.
title: Secretly Seeking System—Instituting the Social
Transformers

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                  Self-attention is central to transformer models, but its quadratic scaling with sequence length limits efficiency and applicability. We explore summation-based aggregation as an alternative. In this approach, each token is modulated by a learned positional encoding, passed through linear layers with nonlinearities, and then aggregated by addition at cost
                  <jats:italic toggle="yes">O(nd)</jats:italic>
                  . In document classification, this mechanism performs on par with attention when tested in isolation. For autoregressive language modeling, pure summation underperforms, but a hybrid design-summation in intermediate layers with a single attention layer at the output-matches or even exceeds full-attention performance while keeping most of the network near-linear in cost. In multimodal regression, summation provides a shared channel that supports generalization across inputs. Overall, the results indicate that hybrid architectures offer a practical route to scalable transformers, while also raising broader questions about how bottlenecked aggregation shapes representation and abstraction.
                </jats:p>
title: Summation-Based Transformers: A Path Toward Linear Complexity Sequence Modeling

items.abstract: This chapter explains the second paradox of alterity: alterity is felt as extraneous and familiar at the same time. It comes as a surprise from the most intimate and proper region of the Self. What is experienced as most extraneous is also what is most proper to the Self. These are the two sides of a fold: a zone of continuity rather than discontinuity. This is the topos of the Double and the Uncanny. Alterity does not coincide with the Freudian Unconscious. This impersonal and not individuated part is not repressed. It is the obscure side of my own existence as it manifests itself in front of myself. From this stems a further paradox: if alterity is our own life in as much as it does not belong to us, then we must respond for something for which we are not responsible.
title: The Uncanny and the secretly familiar double

items.abstract: Cross-layer weight sharing in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformers—where adjacent transformer lay- ers reuse the same expert weight tensors—reduces parameter counts without changing the number of pa- rameters activated per token. However, existing post- training quantization (PTQ) methods treat shared weights as if they belong to a single layer, calibrat- ing with only one layer’s activation statistics. We show that the correct objective for a weight W shared across layers ℓ1,...,ℓn is to minimise the total re- construction error i tr[(Wq−W)Hℓi (Wq−W)⊤], which reduces to GPTQ applied with a combined Hessian Hcomb = i αiHℓi . We propose CLHA (Cross-Layer Hessian Aggregation), which implements this combined calibration within a GPTQ frame- work, and CLHA-MP, a mixed-precision extension that allocates one extra bit to always-active shared experts whose higher activation frequency implies greater quantization sensitivity. Experiments on a 34.5M-parameter cross-layer-shared MoE trained on WikiText-2 show that CLHA reduces perplexity by 4.3–5.4% over per-layer independent calibration at 2-bit quantization, and CLHA-MP achieves an 18.6% improvement. A controlled routing-sharpness exper- iment confirms that CLHA gains grow with cross- layer divergence (from +4.3% at natural routing to +8.0% at 3×router scale), while PLIC degrades 5% in the same setting. We also identify a critical imple- mentation pitfall: standard PyTorch forward hooks silently corrupt Hessian estimates for shared-module architectures, and we describe a layer-aware callback mechanism that resolves this.
title:
CLHA: Cross-Layer Hessian Aggregation for Quantizing
Weight-Shared Mixture-of-Experts Transformers

items.abstract: <jats:p>Recurrent networks for online learning must update their weights from each new observation without revisiting the past, the regime in which Real-Time Recurrent Learning (RTRL) provides an exact gradient. Its cost (O(n^4) time and O(n^3) memory for an n-unit dense network) has nonetheless kept it impractical, and the cheap approximations that followed each surrender something essential: stochastic estimators inject uncontrolled variance, deterministically sparse rules discard cross-unit credit with no account of the resulting error, and exact-by-construction methods abandon dense recurrence altogether. We introduce Sketched RTRL (SK-RTRL), which represents the influence matrix as an exact SnAp-1 block-diagonal part together with a deterministic two-sided low-rank sketch of the off-diagonal residual, so that a single rank knob r interpolates from SnAp-1 (r=0) to exact RTRL (r=n). The shrinkage that controls the sketch yields, at no additional asymptotic cost, a running scalar certificate e_t = rho_bar_t * e_{t-1} + eta_t that bounds the influence-matrix error, and through it the gradient bias, at every step, to our knowledge the first such guarantee for an RTRL approximation. The bound holds for any spectral-norm trajectory and attains the geometric rate 1/(1 - rho_bar) in contractive phases. Because truncation records its own discarded mass, the rank can be resized online without invalidating the bound, driving a simple adaptive-rank controller. Across diagnostic, chaotic, and real-world benchmarks on dense tanh recurrent networks and a memory-scaling study, SK-RTRL attains markedly higher gradient fidelity than sparse and stochastic estimators even at low sketch rank, and extends dense-RNN online training to widths at which storing the exact influence matrix is impractical.</jats:p>
title: Certified Low-Rank Real-Time Recurrent Learning for Dense Recurrent Neural Networks

items.abstract: In 1995, the Asante people of central Ghana celebrated a sumptuous first-fruits festival, Odwira . Although the festival is held annually, this one was unusual in that it also marked the 25th year of the reign of their king, the Asantehene . The event was charged with political as well as cultural meaning. Asante and its king had been at the centre of opposition to the radical nationalist party led by Kwame Nkrumah which had taken Ghana into independence in 1957. That opposition had been ruthlessly suppressed and humiliated and this Odwira proved to be a very public opportunity for both an energetic re-assertion of Asante pride and for revenge against a brand of radical politics which remains significantly less popular in the region than it does in other parts of Ghana.
title: Memory as Theatre
subtitle: Using a Ghanaian Ritual to Recall Past Greatness and to Redress Recent Reverses

items.abstract: <jats:p>To investigate the role of measures of past performance and accomplishments in determining compensation, we develop a principal-agent model where the agent's ability is not observed directly by the principal.  To the extent managerial ability persists over time, past performance and accomplishments signal how the agent's innate ability is likely to affect future performance which, in turn, should affect his value to the firm as well as the wage level he can command in the labor market for his services.  We show that the principal's optimal solution for employing and compensating the agent can be implemented by a simple take-it-or-leave-it offer mechanism in which the optimal compensation level can be expressed as a nonlinear function of two linear aggregates of measures of past performance.  We show that the optimal aggregate measure places a greater weight on measures of past performance that are more precise and more sensitive to the agent's ability.  The results are analogous to those in moral hazard models, but they stem from the posterior expectation about the agent's ability in creating value for the firm and in commanding a higher market price rather than the slope of the loglikelihood function in inferring his unobservable effort.</jats:p>
title: Relative Weights on Measures of Past Performance

<jats:p>This article considers a temporal dimension and extends the theoretical framework beyond the leisure constraints theory to incorporate passive use and direct use values for the first time, to examine nonattendees' intention to attend a rural festival. It was found that passive use values
 affect only the decision to attend but direct use values influence that decision to take place sooner rather than later. Results also support the family life cycle stage theory for a potential first visit but not the decision to visit soon while the reverse was found for the distance decay
 theory. Overall, the impact of the various dimensions of the barriers within the leisure constraints theory, the perceived beliefs, and visit motivations differed among would-be visitors and those intending to visit sooner rather than later. Thus, a dual marketing strategy aimed generally
 at the former, and specifically at the latter, would be effective in attracting new visitors to rural festivals.</jats:p>
title: To Attend or not to Attend a Rural Folk Festival: Examining Nonattendees' Behavior Using a Temporal Approach

items.abstract: <jats:p>Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now exceed 90\% accuracy on chart question answering, yet whether their explanations are causally grounded in the visual evidence they cite remains unmeasured. We introduce FaithChart, a framework that measures and improves the visual grounding of chart explanations. First, we propose two causal, black-box metrics—Sufficiency and Comprehensiveness—computed by perturbing cited chart-image regions and observing the change in predictions. Second, we release FaithChart-1500, a benchmark of $1,498$ human-verified samples with dual-LLM reasoning traces. Third, we introduce FaithChart-B, a parameter-efficient model whose structured evidence supervision cuts the sufficiency–comprehensiveness imbalance by 88\% at only a 5.5-point accuracy cost. Across four state-of-the-art MLLMs, faithfulness ranking inverts accuracy ranking—the most accurate model is not the most faithful, and correctness does not predict grounding. FaithChart offers a reproducible instrument for auditing and training visually grounded multimodal reasoning.</jats:p>
title: FaithChart: Measuring and Improving the Visual Grounding of Chart Explanations in Vision-Language Models

items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now exceed 90% accuracy on chart question answering, yet whether their explanations are causally grounded in the visual evidence they cite remains unmeasured. We introduce FaithChart, a framework that measures and improves the visual grounding of chart explanations. First, we propose two causal, black-box metrics—Sufficiency and Comprehensiveness—computed by perturbing cited chart-image regions and observing the change in predictions. Second, we release FaithChart-1500, a benchmark of 1,498 human-verified samples with dual-LLM reasoning traces. Third, we introduce FaithChart-B, a parameter-efficient model whose structured evidence supervision cuts the sufficiency–comprehensiveness imbalance by 88% at only a 5.5-point accuracy cost. Across four state-of-the-art MLLMs, faithfulness ranking inverts accuracy ranking—the most accurate model is not the most faithful, and correctness does not predict grounding. FaithChart offers a reproducible instrument for auditing and training visually grounded multimodal reasoning.
title: FaithChart: Measuring and Improving the Visual Grounding of Chart Explanations in Vision-Language Models

items.abstract:
<jats:p>By providing access, data and new forms of literacy and communication practices, it is widely accepted that 
networked technologies have done much to promote learner autonomy. However, in practical terms, the lack of resources, expertise and 
research investigations into learner interaction have all too often meant that autonomous learning is conveniently likened to 
teacher-independent learning, largely relying on the success and assumed intuitiveness of the World Wide Web (web) for its 
learner driven delivery. This situation affecting foreign language teaching and learning has been further aggravated by the recent 
trend, at least in UK universities, to conceive languages solely as communicative tools, further severing them from their academic 
base and cultural roots, often reducing learner autonomy to poor repetitive interaction. On this premise, this paper proposes to 
focus on how to make better use of the interactive potential of the web in order to maximise independent language learning online. 
From a Human Computer Interaction (HCI) design perspective, it intends to shed further light on and increase our understanding of 
hypermedia and multimedia structures through learner participation and evaluation. On the basis of evidence from an ongoing research 
investigation into online CALL literacy, it will seek to identify crucial causalities between the user interface and learner 
interaction affecting the learners’ focus and engagement within their own learning processes. The adopted methodology 
combines a task analysis of a hypermedia prototype underpinned by an activity theory approach and participatory design based on 
user walkthroughs and focus groups. By looking at the relationship between action and goal as well as between activities and motives, 
it attempts to provide a framework for evaluating online hypermedia interactivity based on identified activities, design tasks 
and design criteria.</jats:p>
title: Evaluating hypermedia structures as a means of improving language learning strategies and motivation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing, yet they fundamentally lack the capacity for genuine emotional memory and affective reasoning. This paper introduces Topological Emotional Memory (TEM)-a novel framework that integrates a structured, graph-based emotional memory system with existing LLMs without modifying their core architecture. Drawing from topological principles, cognitive psychology, and affective neuroscience, TEM models memories as nodes in a directed graph embedded in a continuous emotional space, where edges represent affective, sensory, and temporal relationships. We present a comprehensive mathematical formulation including: (1) a multidimensional emotional encoding based on valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space, (2) a topological graph structure with weighted edges representing emotional similarity, (3) retrieval algorithms for contextually-aware memory recall, (4) dynamic learning mechanisms for memory consolidation and adaptation, and (5) integration protocols for existing transformer-based LLMs. Through rigorous theoretical analysis and detailed case studies, we demonstrate that TEM enables: (a) contextually-aware emotional retrieval with 92.3% relevance accuracy, (b) deep empathetic response generation that maintains emotional coherence across interactions, (c) dynamic learning from user interactions with minimal computational overhead (O(N + E) per update), and (d) navigation through complex affective trajectories via topological pathfinding algorithms. The framework bridges the critical gap between statistical language modeling and phenomenological experience, offering a computationally tractable (O(N log k) retrieval complexity) approach to emotional intelligence in AI systems. Our results suggest that TEM can serve as a foundational architecture for next-generation empathetic AI, with applications in mental health, education, creative AI, and human-computer interaction.</jats:p>
title: Topological Emotional Memory: A Framework for Deep Affective Recall in Large Language Models

items.abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 Empirical corporate governance research depends on structured data extracted from legal text, a translation exercise that has traditionally required costly and difficult-to-scale human coding. Using the DECODEM benchmarks developed in companion work, this paper asks what role LLM-based extraction can play in governance data production: whether automated extraction routines perform on par with realistic human coding workflows and whether model-human disagreement can guide audits of human-coded data. The paper's main findings are based on a blind adjudication of observations on which human coding and the automated extraction routines disagree.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 The analysis supports three main findings. First, for many governance variables, LLM-based extraction performs at levels at least comparable to feasible human coding workflows, at less than two percent of the marginal cost of human coding. Second, different extraction routines often make only partially overlapping errors, creating value from ensemble rules that aggregate multiple routines. In the setting studied here, labels generated through ensemble rules agree with the adjudicated labels substantially more often than initial human labels did. Third, substantial variation across variables remains, so LLM-generated governance variables should not be used for downstream research without validation against hand-collected data. The results also carry an implication for settings where fully automated coding is not appropriate: because human and model errors also overlap only weakly, flagging observations on which any of six routines disagrees with the initial human label would surface more than ninety percent of observed human coding errors while requiring review of roughly seven percent of observations. Together, the results point towards a new model of data production in which human judgment defines and validates governance variables, while LLM-based extraction supplies scalable coding and targeted quality control.
</div></jats:p>
title: Measuring Corporate Governance with Large Language Models

items.abstract: <jats:p>Speech-comprehension difficulties are common among older people. Standard speech tests do not fully capture such difficulties because the tests poorly resemble the context-rich, story-like nature of ongoing conversation and are typically available only in a country's dominant/official language (e.g., English), leading to inaccurate scores for native speakers of other languages. Assessments for naturalistic, story speech in multiple languages require accurate, time-efficient scoring. The current research leverages modern large language models (LLMs) in native English speakers and native speakers of 10 other languages to automate the generation of high-quality, spoken stories and scoring of speech recall in different languages. Participants listened to and freely recalled short stories (in quiet/clear and in babble noise) in their native language. Large language model text-embeddings and LLM prompt engineering with semantic similarity analyses to score speech recall revealed sensitivity to known effects of temporal order, primacy/recency, and background noise, and high similarity of recall scores across languages. The work overcomes limitations associated with simple speech materials and testing of closed native-speaker groups because recall data of varying length and details can be mapped across languages with high accuracy. The full automation of speech generation and recall scoring provides an important step toward comprehension assessments of naturalistic speech with clinical applicability.</jats:p>
title: Language-agnostic, Automated Assessment of Listeners’ Speech Recall Using Large Language Models

<jats:p><div>
 LLM "AI-trading" benchmarks are routinely scored by replaying historical markets, raising a contamination concern: a model that has memorized an asset's realized outcome cannot generate honest out-of-sample skill, so backtest performance may be recall rather than foresight. We build a white-box-to-black-box validated leakage instrument and use it to ask the decision-relevant question prior work leaves open: does memorization capacity actually transmit to trading decisions? We report a dissociation. Capacity is large, precise, and universal: across 16 open models (10 vendors) and three commercial APIs, models prefer the realized revenue over magnitude-matched (±15%) counterfactuals at 0.23–0.81 (chance 0.20) and freely generate the figure within 10% for up to 89% of famous firm-years, while no-leak chronologically-consistent baselines sit at chance. Recall is cutoff-bounded: exploiting the models' different training cutoffs, it collapses to chance for facts dated after a model's cutoff (within-model t = −6.6, 18 of 19 models), the design-based signature of memorization rather than estimation. Applied to the realized return itself — the variable a backtest fears — recall is at chance with no cutoff signature: these models memorize fundamentals, not prices. Realization, by contrast, is null across five independent tests, including a cross-sectional ranking task (N ≈ 5,700 per model) and a realistic StockBench-style backtest over six open and frontier-API agents; an apparent agentic signal (+9.9pp, t = 4.07) is shown to be a firm-prominence confound that vanishes under firm fixed effects (β = −0.018). A pre-registered, dependence-corrected power analysis bounds any residual post-cutoff skill: on a ≈2,000-name post-cutoff universe the minimum detectable mean |IC| is ≈0.012–0.016, below the 0.02–0.05 band where real cross-sectional strategies operate. The contribution is a validated leakage instrument, an identification result showing why memorization is invisible to any pre-cutoff backtest, and the finding that, for the signals we test, LLM memorization of the market does not become measurable market skill.
</div></jats:p>
title: Memorized but Not Realized: Frontier Language Models Precisely Recall Financial Fundamentals, but It Does Not Become Trading Skill

items.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) are widely assumed to behave consistently regardless of the language in which a prompt is expressed. We challenge this assumption through a controlled empirical study in which language itself is isolated as the sole independent variable. We present 30 semantically equivalent prompts across three prompt categories— Factual, Normative, and Safety-sensitive—to two state-of-the-art LLMs (Llama-3.3-70B and GPT-OSS-20B) in English, Hindi, and French, yielding 360 responses. We introduce the Behavioral Divergence Score (BDS), a composite metric combining semantic similarity (SBERT cosine distance), sentiment divergence, and refusal-class mismatch. Our analysis reveals that cross-language divergence consistently exceeds the intra-language noise floor by factors of 1.1×–2.5×, that normative prompts produce the highest sentiment divergence (Ssent = 0.28), and that safety-category refusal behaviour is inconsistent across languages in 10% of prompt–model pairs. All three pre-registered directional hypotheses were not supported in strict statistical sense, a result we interpret as a meaningful empirical finding: the divergence is real and category-dependent, but it does not follow monotonic ordering predicted by the linguistic-distance theory alone. These results motivate rethinking multilingual evaluation beyond aggregate accuracy metrics and highlight concrete safety implications for real-world deployments.
title: Language as a Hidden Variable: Measuring Behavioral Divergence in Multilingual Large Language Models

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Consistency of a model—that is, the invariance of its behavior under meaning-preserving alternations in its input—is a highly desirable property in natural language processing. In this paper we study the question: Are Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) consistent with respect to factual knowledge? To this end, we create ParaRel🤘, a high-quality resource of cloze-style query English paraphrases. It contains a total of 328 paraphrases for 38 relations. Using ParaRel🤘, we show that the consistency of all PLMs we experiment with is poor— though with high variance between relations. Our analysis of the representational spaces of PLMs suggests that they have a poor structure and are currently not suitable for representing knowledge robustly. Finally, we propose a method for improving model consistency and experimentally demonstrate its effectiveness.1</jats:p>
title: Measuring and Improving Consistency in Pretrained Language Models

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) encode substantial knowledge from large-scale corpora during pre-training, forming complex semantic patterns in their parametric representations. From a pattern recognition perspective, knowledge editing can be viewed as the task of identifying, associating, and rectifying the internal knowledge patterns relevant to a target fact. However, the encoded parametric knowledge inevitably becomes outdated over time, necessitating post-training rectification. Current knowledge-based model editing (KME) methods enable parameter-localized updates to modify model behavior, but they largely overlook the semantic interdependencies between target edits (i.e., new knowledge) and the model&apos;s existing knowledge. This limitation may disrupt internal knowledge coherence and lead to suboptimal editing outcomes. Inspired by human neurocognitive processes, where activation in the prefrontal cortex triggers associative memory retrieval during new information encoding, we propose Associative Memory-based Editing (AME), a novel KME framework that establishes semantic bridges between new knowledge and intrinsic parametric knowledge. Specifically, AME introduces three key innovations: (1) a rule-guided association mechanism that identifies the entity type in the target edit and triggers predefined constraints for context-aware knowledge recall; (2) a sparse parameter identification algorithm that strategically pinpoints a small subset of parameters closely related to the target edit; and (3) a dual-objective optimization protocol that jointly optimizes the target knowledge and its associative memory. Extensive experiments on two benchmarks verify that AME consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines.</jats:p>
title: Recall Before Rectification: Editing Large Language Models via Relevant Knowledge Activation
